newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS - FEB 6.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS - FEB 6.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek financial press:

--Deputy Development Minister in charge of trade Mihalis Chrysohoides will present plans to revise the procurements programme for the public sector - worth 1.5 trillion annually - to Prime Minister Costas Simitis within the next few days. The plan will attempt to bring some uniformity to contracts with the state, universities, hospitals, state pensions funds and a myriad number of other institutions and bodies.

--Wage increases will hinder the further fall of inflation and any increase in jobs, the OECD's latest six-monthly report on Greece says. Despite reservations about inflation and deficits, however, the report was positive about developments in the economy.

--There are reports that Olympic Airways, Greece's national carrier, is heading for its 31st board of directors since coming under state control in 1975. However, OA's president, managing consultant and general director all denied being asked for their resignations, saying there had been a 'misunderstanding'.
--The possibility of a compromise with strikers sought by both the economy and the markets appears to be receding as both government and strikers harden their stance.
--Meanwhile, the inner cabinet meeting yesterday decided that it had to keep the national roads open at all costs and to rally the members of ruling party PASOK to support the government.

--Both the European Commission's report on Greece and the OECD report find positive developments in the deficits-inflation front, as well as noting a significant increase in GDP growth. The OECD, however, warned of new dangers to competitiveness.

--Greeks come second to last (above Portugal) in purchasing power among all European Union countries, according to Eurostat. Greeks' purchasing power is about one-third less than that of the average European.
--Tear-gas and fire-hoses may be used by riot police stationed in Thessaly to keep national roads open, the inner cabinet reportedly decided at its hurriedly-covened meeting yesterday.
--The national economy ministry is putting together a report on the absorption rates of EU funds for EU commissioner Monika Wulf-Mathies, who will be visiting Greece on February 19th.

--The hour of truth: Prime Minister Costas Simitis reportedly told his ministers that they needed to rally and support the government's policies, stressing that the future of the government and the country was at stake.

--The farmers' protests will continue despite disagreements in the ranks. Farmers want a meeting with Simitis today or tomorrow. Today's developments are expected to be decisive for the protests as protesters will either abandon efforts or mass to close the roads.
--Plans to build a chain of shopping centres around the country were presented to the public yesterday by the director of the Cohesion Fund, which fully subsidised the report.

--A new Eurobank will emerge from talks between Eurobank and Interbank, according to reports. The new improved bank will offer more services and products and will increase its bracnh network. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
